newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stocks leap on U.S. rally, Tokyo rebounds.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stocks leap on U.S. rally, Tokyo rebounds.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks led the upswing in most Asian markets on Friday, fired by a surge in U.S. shares overnight.
But gains in Tokyo were capped by ongoing gloom about the outlook for Japan's anaemic economy.

Bangkok and Singapore stocks were the only losers. Both markets sagged on domestic factors with Bangkok reeling from an exodus of foreign money. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index posted its biggest point gain in more than two years as investors cheered a drop in U.S. bond yields and a surge in Wall Street stocks overnight.
The Hang Seng Index surged 284.85 points, or 2.22 percent, to 13,131.41. The rise was the biggest since August 30, 1994, when the index rose 287.48 points.
"We have a double whammy -- a very strong bond market and a strong Wall Street," said Geoff Galbraith, institutional sales trader at Nava SC Securities.
The U.S. long bond jumped 1-16/32 on Thursday to yield 6.59 percent while the Dow industrials posted their second-largest net gain ever, rising 126.87 points to 6,473.64.
Wall Street's rally gave Tokyo stocks a reason to bounce back from a three-day losing streak, but shares struggled to stay in positive territory and brokers said the turnaround could be shortlived.
The economic worries that sent stocks spiralling 2.6 percent to their lowest close in a year on Thursday were still hanging over the market.
Brokers said the overall direction was still downward.
The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed up 0.61 percent, or 119.79 points, at 19,690.46.
Australian shares sprinted home to close sharply higher at 2,373.8, a gain of 42.1 points, inspired by New York's performance.
In turnover terms, the Australian market set new records with A$1.73 billion (US$1.38 billion) worth of shares traded, surpassing the previous record of A$1.6 billion on June 28, 1996.
Seoul's market ended higher on talk that pension funds entered the market to buy cheap, heavily weighted, large-cap shares, brokers said.
The composite stock index gained 9.90 points to close at 700.87.
Bombay's 30-share index jumped 52.62 points, or 1.73 percent, to a provisional close of 3,088.53 on fund buying and short-covering, brokers said.
They said sentiment was boosted by the resignation of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao from his last party post as chief of the Congress party's parliamentary team on Thursday.
Manila's market got an early lift from Wall Street but late profit-taking trimmed gains, brokers said. The composite index ended up 25.82 points, or 0.82 percent, at 3,180.20.

Jakarta share prices made gains in active trading as the index climbed on the back of rises in some heavyweights, including Telkom, brokers said. The Jakarta Composite Index rose 4.21 points, or 0.67 percent, to end at 632.52 points.
Taiwan share prices also closed higher, helped by Wall Street but rising mainly on news that local regulators had raised the stock investment ceiling for individual foreign funds, brokers said.
The weighted index ended up 31.26 points or 0.46 percent at 6,890.66.
New Zealand shares also benefited from the U.S. rally, with the NZSE-40 Capital Index ending 14.08 points higher at 2,349.98.
Malaysia's Composite Index finished at 1,203.06, up 2.03 points.
But Wall Street's cheer failed to buoy Thai stocks. The SET Index finished down 15.81 points, or 1.90 percent, at 816.79.
"I think the market just has no positive news, I think the foreigners were still the main sellers," said Somchai Traitrattanapirom, vice-president at Sitca Investment and Securities.
Singapore shares ended mildly weaker after the release of November trade data where non-oil domestic exports saw an unexpected sharp fall of 8.8 percent.
The Straits Times Industrial index ended 2.54 points lower at 2,196.81.
One dealer said some funds fleeing Thailand's plunging stock market had made their way into the Singapore market.
SIMEX Brent crude futures gave up ground, as players squared positions ahead of the holiday.
February Brent was last traded at US$23.73 per barrel, down 25 cents from the London settlement on Thursday.
Hong Kong gold ended another listless session unchanged at US$369.00/50 against New York's Thursday close.
At 1119 GMT, the dollar was trading at 114.23/33 yen and 1.5563/69 marks after sluggish Tokyo activity.
